project_title: Custom Beverage Mixing Device Prototype (DJ-Style Matcha Mixer)
question: Combine the pre-task requirement state with the current client task. If the task determines a unique post-task state, choose ACT and construct that state; otherwise choose CLARIFY and identify the blocking requirement field and the question that must be answered.

target_task.speaker: client
target_task.text:
I’m good with this direction because the additional power and adjustable speed range make sense. The 5200 RPM motors work for me as long as we do not run them at maximum continuously; being able to dial them down for slow mixing or increase them for higher-speed frothing is ideal.

With that higher maximum, however, we need to ensure two things:
• splashing remains under control
• mixing stays smooth rather than becoming overly aggressive at higher speeds

If necessary, I’m open to adding a splash guard or adjusting the whisk position and bowl depth so the machine continues to operate cleanly. Overall, I approve this approach.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: For a quickly developed initial prototype, Elena, I can cover both the mechanical and electrical work without a problem. I do not expect the motors to need any metal mounting hardware because the proposed mounting approach should handle their torque easily. A 7-9 week timeline would be comfortable for me.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Stability will come from a solid base fitted with rubber/TPU feet, which should stop the unit from rattling or shifting. On the electronics side, the first build will stay as simple as possible and use off-the-shelf components. Selecting a motor that easily handles the liquid load should also make the mixing reliable. I could provide an initial BOM within 72-96 hours.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text:
This approach and timeline sound great, Nolan, so let’s move forward.

The first step should cover:
• system layout
• motor + component selection
• basic wiring plan

From there, the goal is to get a working prototype running as quickly as possible and refine it afterward. Tell me what information you need from me to begin.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I’m ready to proceed whenever you are, Elena, and everything is prepared on my end. Before starting, I have one final question about power: should the unit plug into a standard 120v wall outlet, or would you prefer 12v power like a car battery? I’m ready to begin the CAD work and assemble the bill of materials, and I’ll promptly let you know if any other questions arise. Thank you—I look forward to working with you on the project.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: For the initial version, let’s use a standard 120V wall outlet. Since it will be used at events, I want this version to remain as simple and reliable as possible; battery power can be explored later. Everything sounds good from my side, and I’m excited to begin. As you start the CAD and BOM, let me know what you need from me.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: The selected setup works for me, Elena. I’ll implement 120v wall power while leaving open the option to adapt or change it to a 12v battery later if needed. I’ll start the CAD and BOM now, and as soon as you send the contract over, I can begin project work today. Looking forward to it!

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: The contract is being prepared now, and I’ll send it over next Friday once it is ready. I’m looking forward to working with you.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I appreciate it, Elena, and I’m looking forward to working with you as well.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Hello Nolan,

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: The contract has been included as an attachment.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I’ve reviewed the contract, Elena, and both the document and its terms look good to me. I agree to them. One important note: to make the arrangement official on upwork, you’ll need to submit it through their system using the hire button. The proposal I originally sent can be edited to include your milestones.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: This is my first time hiring through Upwork, Nolan. Thanks for the guidance—I’m completing the process now.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I completely understand, so there’s no need to worry.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Should I attach the contract after I click the Hire button?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: You can attach the contract, but the milestones should also be entered into the official upwork contract.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Can the contract be attached in the first section? I also noticed a separate Milestones tab—do I need to create another Milestones PDF and upload it there?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: In the first section, you can add the PDF; in the following section, enter the milestones already written into the contract. My Upwork experience has only been as someone working for clients, not hiring them, so I’m not 100% certain what the process looks like from your side.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: I'm completing the hiring process now.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I appreciate it, Elena. I’ll begin the work and keep you informed as it progresses.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Great! Thanks.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: By next Thursday, I should have the initial BOM completed. After that, I’ll rough out the CAD, but final measurements and exact component placement cannot be determined until I physically receive the components.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: One additional requirement came up later that I forgot to mention. In the attached image, the matcha mixer has no actual way to pour its contents. Please add a spout at the bottom, oriented toward the barista so pouring is easier.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Is the proposed approach feasible, or would another method work better?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Although it makes the design somewhat more complicated, the proposed approach should be feasible.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: What makes the proposed spout more difficult?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Unless I’ve misunderstood, the motor is intended to sit beneath the bowl while the mixing head protrudes through its bottom. My current plan is therefore to place a hole directly in the bowl’s center for that mechanism. The drainage opening would need to be offset from the center hole, which may leave some liquid behind even after the bowl has fully drained.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Could we find a workaround that still keeps the process smooth and efficient?

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Suppose we update the design to resemble this reference. A) Would that improve pouring efficiency? B) Would the build become simpler? C) Would the project timeframe change?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: With this alternative design, pouring would be more efficient and the build would be simpler. The reason is that we would no longer need to manage possible leakage through a shaft seal, as the other method requires. Switching to this approach should not negatively affect the timeframe.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Let’s adopt this design while retaining the DJ Turntables vibe. The pour spot should face the baristas, all buttons need to be functional, and splashing should be minimized as much as possible. Keep the existing words on the machine unchanged, apart from the title, which should read "Elena's Chai Whisk," and use green accents. I also want to retain the thickness shown in the side view. The matcha wells should be deep, but the box itself must not become too large.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: For V1, what simple, reliable implementation approach would you use for the spout? It must provide a smooth, controlled pour while remaining easy to clean between uses. A proper seal should prevent liquid from leaking into the base, and the open/close mechanism needs to operate cleanly without dripping.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text:
Key Design Details

1\. Valve / flow control — I need a simple open/close valve or tap that prevents constant dripping and uncontrolled pouring.

2\. Seal at the bottom — This is critical: the bottom bowl seal must prevent external leaks as well as seepage into the electronics.

3\. Cleaning — Because matcha + milk leaves residue, the spout should either be removable or easy to flush and clean.

4\. Flow rate — I need a smooth, controlled stream rather than a slow drip or an explosive pour.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I’m reviewing everything here and will return shortly with a fresh design approach. Before that, I need to confirm one more design detail: how much matcha should each bowl mix at once? I’m currently considering 12qt bowls, which would support approx 11qt of matcha per bowl. Does that sound like the right capacity, or should I adjust it upward or downward?

messages.speaker: client
messages.text:
Rather than increasing capacity to 12qt, I prefer the smaller bowls shown in the earlier design. Refilling is acceptable because the priorities are:
• better mixing quality
• consistent foam
• faster visual cycles during events

12 qt's would look like the attached picture, and bowls that large detract from the design and aesthetic. Let’s use a smaller bowl matching the size in the earlier pictures; I don’t mind refilling it.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: With the smaller capacity, please make one additional adjustment: the bowls should be easy to remove and quick to swap. That will let me prepare bowls in advance and exchange them rapidly during events.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: The bowl size shown here is acceptable. For the design color, though, I’d like to use beige.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: understood.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Taking the recent design requirements into account, I’ve prepared the initial BOM for your review. Additional wires, hardware, and the custom-fabricated housing are not included yet, although I already have their materials in my shop; they will be added after the build begins. I’m now starting the initial cad design with rough component measurements. Once you approve and purchase the components, I can measure each physical piece accurately and fully refine the design. All components have been sourced from amazon so future changes or additions can be handled quickly.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text:
For review, the component breakdown is as follows:

Vessels: 4.5-Quart Stainless Steel Bowls (Qty 2) - $21.18. These serve as the main mixing reservoirs. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00B4GTH0I>

Motors: 12V 450RPM Gear Motors (Qty 2) - $37.46. These are the high-speed mixing drive units. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B072R5QSRG>

Drivetrain: 1/2" Shaft Couplings (Qty 2) - $14.82. Each coupling links a motor to its extension shaft. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0D6XMSSFY>

Drivetrain: 1/2" x 14" 304 Stainless Steel Shafts (Qty 2) - $7.86. These extend from the motors to the whisks. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DXPPL2LL>

Agitators: Wire Whisks (Qty 2) - $21.50. Their high-aeration heads provide mixing and frothing. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B078SL7D5L>

Control: PWM DC Speed Controllers (Qty 2) - $14.38. These give users independent control of vortex speed. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B09LS3ZWP9>

Power: 12V 35A DC Power Supply (Qty 1) - $10.49. This line provides the main power source for the electronics. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08Y64DTK8>

Cooling: 80mm 12V Cooling Fans (Qty 2) - $15.98. The fans handle enclosure thermal management. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0FBFK9F4Y>

Structural: Brass Bulkhead Fittings 3/4" F to 1" M (Qty 2) - $9.16. These create through-bowl mounts for the drive shafts. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B09GVB9VLM>

Plumbing: 3/8" ID Silicone Tubing 18ft (Qty 1) - $7.15. This tubing forms the main transfer path from each bowl to its spigot. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B089YG7TWB>

Adapters: SS 3/8" Barb to 1" GHT Female (Qty 2) - $13.74. These adapt the spigot’s male threads to the tubing. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0GCDPCLNZ>

Coupling: 3/4" Barb Unions (Qty 2) - $4.49. The unions provide modular break points for cleaning. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0FH4FHV9Y>

Dispensing: Push-Style Beverage Spigots (Qty 2) - $7.50. These form the user-facing dispensing interface. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08TVMD767>

Sealing: #5 Silicone Stopper 3/8" Hole (Qty 5) - $11.48. The friction-fit outlet seal prevents bowl leakage. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DP43QKHG>

Connection: 3/8" Barb to 3/4" NPT Adapter (Qty 2) - $7.48. This creates a rigid interface through the stopper. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DZPBSW8J>

The Estimated Component Total is $204.67.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Power for the electronics comes from a 120v-to-12v 35A DC supply, with each station using its own PWM speed controller. At each station, a 12v 450rpm motor connects through a 1/2" shaft coupling to a 1/2" stainless steel shaft, which drives the wire whisk for mixing and frothing the matcha. The electronics are actively cooled by 80mm fans. In the plumbing system, every 4.5 quart stainless steel bowl has a 3/8 barb outlet, where a #5 silicone stopper creates a press-fit, leak-proof connection. From the barb union inside that stopper, 3/8 silicone tubing runs to the 1" ght adapter, which threads directly onto the push-style beverage spigot.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Until I complete the initial CAD, some aspects will remain easier to understand in the finished model. I shared the expected materials beforehand so you can raise questions or suggest changes while I continue working on the design.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Hello, Nolan,

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Because we are whisking a fine powder, the current whisk is too large. The selected bowls are 4.5qt, while those whisks are intended for 10qt bowls. We need to replace them with something smaller and thinner.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Could the spout be revised to match the diagram more closely? I’m unsure whether Matcha will retain the same consistency after running through the proposed spout, and it will not preserve the frothiness.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Here is the external product reference for the required whisk design: <https://www.amazon.com/Matcha-Reusable-Stirring-Japanese-Ceremony/dp/B0F3JBJ74L/ref=sr_1_22?s=home-garden&sr=1-22>

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: For the whisk we need, please follow the style shown in this reference. That type of whisk performs better with fine powder.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Regarding the whisk, understood—I’ll source a more suitable option for that component. The spout shown in your image is possible, but reproducing it would require us to rethink the design, develop custom circuitry, and do additional custom work. To make matcha flow through that type of spout on demand, we would essentially need a solenoid that opens and closes a valve inside the dispensing mechanism. Developing a reliable solution would involve custom mechanical parts, wiring, and some R&D, so it would likely push us beyond the timeline for this 1st edition. Several off-the-shelf spout alternatives are available, though. Could one of those work instead?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Here is the off-the-shelf beverage-spout search reference: <https://www.amazon.com/s?k=beverage+spout>

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Greetings, Nolan,

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Because dispensing the Matcha through a spout would make it lose its consistency, I don’t think that is the best approach. Could we create a gravity-based dispensing method instead?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Although this is a significant change to the engineering scope, I can make it work. I haven’t been able to find an off-the-shelf spout that closely matches the appearance of the one in your renders, but I did find an option that should function well. A solenoid valve would sit directly beneath the bowl, preventing any matcha from entering the spout until the button is pressed; releasing the button would stop the pour. Since no matcha would remain in either the spout or the tubing, its frothiness will be maintained. Please review this option: <https://www.amazon.com/Stainless-Pourers-BALTRE-Vinegar-Suitable> Alternatively, if keeping the appearance of the original rendered spout is more important, I could fabricate a custom version, though it would not be made from steel.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: After giving it more thought and doing further research, I’ve revised my assessment: I believe I could fabricate the spouts from stainless steel myself while making them look quite similar to the rendering you supplied.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Go ahead with that approach, and please match the rendering as closely as possible; I really like both its appearance and functionality. I do want one change from the rendering: move the plate labeled "Elena's Chai Whisk" from the back of the machine to the front. The spout and mixers will face the baristas, while customers will view the machine from another angle, so the "Elena's Chai Whisk" plate needs to face the customer.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: I’ll make those changes. Both the revised build strategy and the revamped BOM are nearly finished.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Ok.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: To accommodate the new spout and solenoid valve, I’ve revised the original build plan while keeping its general approach. A stainless-steel bulkhead threads into the opening at the bottom of the bowl, and a stainless-steel nipple attached to it forms a quick-release mechanism so the bowls can be swapped easily. Sliding that nipple into the silicone plug creates a watertight seal. On the plug’s opposite side, a 3/4 inch 90 degree connector leads to the solenoid valve. Pressing the button will actuate that valve and dispense the matcha through the stainless-steel spout.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: The exact whisks you previously showed me should be suitable for integration into the setup. Because they are roughly 3/4 the size of the wire whisk we originally planned, I expect them to work nicely with the 4.5qt bowls.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: For review, here is the newly suggested BOM I’ve provided:

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Could you send me a design mock-up showing the whisk you intend to use?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: For the intended design, I would use the exact whisk you recommended yesterday from Amazon. I haven’t supplied the mock-up yet, but connecting that whisk to the steel mixing rod should only require a small, fairly simple adapter.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text:
Hey Nolan — overall, the BOM is exactly the direction I was hoping for, and I really like it. Before we finalize anything, though, I’d like your input on a few details:

• Motors — could 450 RPM be too low for producing a strong, frothy matcha texture? Would increasing the speed make sense if we can still retain enough torque for smooth mixing?

• Whisk — in terms of consistency, durability, and foam quality, would a stainless-steel or milk-frother-style head perform better than the resin whisk?

• Spout — I want to keep the solenoid approach. For both texture and the overall visual experience, the pour needs to remain clean, controlled, and seamless: mix → open → pour.

• Splash / mess control — events make this especially important. The design should provide:
– minimal to no splashing during mixing
– a smooth, controlled spout flow without sputtering
– no dripping while the valve is closed
– effective sealing so liquid cannot leak into the base
– a splash guard or lip around the bowl if needed

• Cleaning — if possible, the bowls and spout components should either be removable or easy to clean.

Everything else looks great. What are your thoughts on these points, and would you adjust anything before we finalize the BOM?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text:
On the motor question, I agree that more speed is appropriate, so I’ve selected replacements that spin at 1800RPM. The PWM controller will provide continuous adjustment from 0 RPM up to 1800 while preserving enough torque to mix the liquids.

Choosing the whisk is more difficult because few available options satisfy all of our requirements. We need a reasonably large mixing head so the entire bowl mixes consistently. The bowl is approximately 13 inch in diameter, whereas the plastic head currently listed on the BOM measures only about 3.6" diameter. By comparison, the original wire whisk I proposed was roughly 6.25" in diameter. Although that whisk is marketed for a 10qt bowl, I think it could still work well in our smaller bowl. A head resembling those on handheld electric frothers or mixers would probably be ideal, but those products are only available in very small sizes.

Splashing is not something I currently expect to be a problem. If the mixing becomes too rough, the motor speed can be adjusted during operation; should testing reveal splashing, we can also install the simple splash guard you suggested.

Cleaning has been considered as well. The bowl is already designed for very easy removal, and I also intend to make the custom spout removable so it can be cleaned easily.

Overall, we are nearly ready, and I’ll update the motor specification to 1800rpm. For the whisk, perhaps we should test 2 styles before choosing the best performer? It is one of the easiest components to exchange for a different design, and a simple adapter should allow us to attach virtually any whisk to the setup.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Another possible whisk has turned up on Amazon. It matches the resin whisk’s diameter but is made from stainless steel, and I could adapt it to the shaft after cutting off its handle: <https://www.amazon.com/Digead-Stainless-Versatile-Blending-Whisking/dp/B088TH4QDV>

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: The whisk works for me. For the motors, I propose setting the maximum speed at 2600—what do you think?

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Yes, that works. Since the knobs can manually limit the operating speed, the extra capacity simply gives us more headroom to test and determine the right setting.

messages.speaker: client
messages.text: Great.

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Because I’m having trouble locating a suitable motor in the 2600 range, I recommend using these 5200RPM motors instead. They will remain fully adjustable from 0 RPM to the 5200rpm maximum. Compared with the models suggested previously, these are slightly larger and should withstand extended use better; their shafts can also be shortened to the required length. <https://www.amazon.com/Motor-3000RPM-Output-Replacement-Electric/dp/B0GCZS9PVK>

messages.speaker: freelancer
messages.text: Because the CAD work is still at a very early stage, the sharp angles and other provisional details will be refined later.
